strengths: Provides a rigorous theoretical framework for coordination among value-maximizing auto-bidders in repeated second-price auctions.
Derives a sharp necessary and sufficient condition (Assumption 1) for coordination to reduce RoS violation for every bidder for any overbidding algorithm.
Proves that mirror-descent-based coordinated bidding increases total value without distributional assumptions and achieves optimal coalition value under Assumption 1.
Extends results to non-i.i.d. valuations, showing robustness of coordination benefits.
Experiments on synthetic and real-world data empirically validate the theoretical predictions.
weaknesses: Ethical and legal concerns: The proposed coordination mechanism is essentially bid suppression/collusion, which can harm seller revenue and outside bidders. The paper does not discuss potential illegality, platform policy violations, or negative societal impacts, nor does it analyze welfare beyond coalition members.

Practical relevance is limited: The mechanism requires a central coordinator with access to all bidders' private values, which is unrealistic for independent advertisers; the paper only briefly mentions this as future work.

Experimental evaluation is narrow: It only compares coordination to independent bidding, does not test cases where Assumption 1 fails (where coordination can hurt utility), does not compare to other coordination mechanisms, and the real-data experiment uses a simplified i.i.d. model based on winning prices rather than true valuations.
The theoretical results are asymptotic (T→∞), and finite-time performance is not analyzed; the experiments use relatively short horizons.
Presentation issues: Several typos and minor errors (e.g., 'coodination', 'seperately', 'monotonicaly', floating 'T' in appendix), and some notation is unclear.
No code or data availability statement, limiting reproducibility of the experiments.

strengths: The paper formalizes a clear and practically motivated question: how coordination among value-maximizing auto-bidders under RoS constraints compares to independent bidding, and it distinguishes its value-maximizer setting from the utility-maximizer collusion literature.

The theory is (to my reading) correct and reasonably complete: Theorem 3.1 provides a clean necessary-and-sufficient condition (Assumption 1) under which coordination improves every coalition bidder's utility, with proofs, and the results extend to non-i.i.d. valuations (Section 5).

Theorems 4.1 and 4.2 give a nontrivial mechanism-level characterization for mirror-descent auto-bidders, identifying a stable reference multiplier and arguing that internal competition raises payments and drives independent bidders to less aggressive multipliers.
Experiments on synthetic data and the public iPinYou dataset are consistent with the theoretical predictions, and confidence intervals are reported.
weaknesses: Limited novelty/significance: the coordination protocol (suppress internal competition so only the highest-value bidder bids) is essentially classic collusion in a second-price auction, and the main results follow fairly directly from the DSIC property of second-price auctions (Lemma 3.1) and from standard mirror-descent convergence arguments. The incremental contribution over known collusion results is modest.

The 'optimality' result (Theorem 4.2) is somewhat vacuous: it shows that the asymptotically best coordination is to drive multipliers to zero (bid to infinity) and always win, which is an obvious consequence of value maximization with a total-utility constraint rather than a deep structural insight. The optimal mechanism degenerates rather than illuminating a rich design space.

The necessity direction of Assumption 1 (Δ<0) is established only via a contrived, hand-crafted algorithm (Appendix A.2), so the claimed 'necessary and sufficient' characterization is weaker than advertised.

Real-world validation is weak and partly circular: values are drawn i.i.d. from the empirical distribution of observed winning prices, which is exactly the i.i.d. model, and the outside bid is an arbitrary scaling by U[1,2]. This does not test realistic market conditions, unobserved bidder heterogeneity, or the robustness claimed in the abstract; it mainly re-confirms the theory on a different marginal distribution.

The model treats the outside bid as an exogenous, non-strategic process, ignoring that external auto-bidders, other coalitions, and the platform will respond to coordination. This is acknowledged only briefly in future work but materially limits the significance of the dominance claims.

Ethical/legal implications are under-addressed: coordinated bidding in ad auctions is functionally collusion, which is illegal in many jurisdictions and harmful to platforms and non-coordinating advertisers. The paper frames coordination as beneficial and offers it as 'useful guidance for industrial practice' without any substantive discussion of legality, detection, or welfare consequences for other market participants.

Presentation problems: numerous typos ('seperately', 'coodination', 'monotonicaly', 'b(e)low'), a notation error in Eq. (1) (max over [N]\{t} instead of [N]\{i}), very small/hard-to-read figures, and main-text proof sketches that are hand-wavy and rely on claims deferred to the appendix.

The empirical evaluation is thin: only one coordination mechanism and one auto-bidding algorithm (entropy mirror map) are tested, no baselines other than independent bidding, and no stress tests of Assumption 1 violations despite the theory emphasizing that regime.

strengths: The paper opens a genuinely new and well-motivated direction: coordination among value-maximizing auto-bidders (as opposed to the standard independent-bidding or utility-maximizing-coordination settings). The two motivating scenarios (a third-party agent managing several advertisers, and one advertiser running several campaigns) are realistic and make the model relevant to practice.

Theorem 3.1 gives a crisp, complete characterization: Assumption 1 is both necessary and sufficient for coordination to reduce every coalition bidder's RoS violation, holding for any weakly-overbidding algorithm. The positive direction (Lemmas 3.1 and 3.2) is clean, and the negative direction (Appendix A.2) constructs a concrete overbidding algorithm showing the assumption cannot be dropped.

Theorem 4.1 is a strong, essentially assumption-free statement: for the broad mirror-descent family (Algorithm 3) coordination weakly improves total coalition value with no distributional condition. The proof idea (reduction to the single-bidder problem with value v_(N), monotonicity of G, potential-function/occupation-measure arguments) is technically substantive and largely rigorous.

Theorem 4.2 establishes asymptotic optimality of the simple highest-value-compete mechanism among *all* coordination mechanisms under Assumption 1, and Section 5 extends the analysis to non-i.i.d. valuations (Theorems 5.1, 5.2), demonstrating robustness. The boundary case λ_* = 0 is treated separately in Appendix B.2, which is thorough.

Experiments on synthetic (symmetric and asymmetric) and iPinYou data are consistent with the theory, showing both higher utility (lower RoS violation) and higher achieved value under coordination, with confidence intervals reported over 100 runs.
weaknesses: The 'real-world' experiment is heavily modeled and does not really validate 'realistic market conditions' as claimed. Values are drawn i.i.d. from the pooled empirical winning-price distribution, and the outside bid is that same distribution rescaled by U[1,2]. This is essentially a synthetic experiment whose only data-derived component is a marginal distribution, and the dramatic gap reported (e.g., value 0.620 -> 0.928) is driven by the artificial U[1,2] scaling. The abstract's claim of validation 'under realistic market conditions' is overstated.

No discussion of the regulatory/ethical dimension. The proposed mechanism is effectively bidder collusion (a cartel), yet the paper only measures coalition welfare. It does not analyze the effect on platform revenue, outside bidders, or social welfare, even though the gains likely come at the expense of these parties. For a paper whose subject is coordinated bidding, the absence of any ethics/limitations discussion is a material omission.

The proof of Lemma 3.1 is stated as a direct consequence of second-price dominant-strategy incentive compatibility, but the competing bids differ between the truthful and independent scenarios (others bid v_j vs b_j), so the DSIC argument as literally written does not apply. The result is in fact true (it follows from a case analysis using b_j >= v_j), but the proof glosses over this.

Some technical conditions used in the proofs are not reflected in the theorem statements. Theorem 4.1 is advertised as requiring no assumptions, yet Lemma B.1 needs the outside bid distribution to have positive density (f_D > 0) and full support. Also, Lemma B.6 asserts G(λ) >= Δ > 0 under Assumption 1, but Assumption 1 only gives Δ >= 0, so the strict-positivity driving the multipliers-to-0 argument in Theorem 4.2 is not fully covered at the boundary Δ = 0.

The empirical evaluation is narrow: only the entropy mirror map instance of Algorithm 3 is tested, with no comparison to other overbidding algorithms, no direct empirical test of the necessity of Assumption 1, and no comparison against alternative coordination mechanisms. This limits how much the experiments corroborate the breadth of the theoretical claims.

Several presentation/notation errors: the competing-bid definition uses max_{j in [N]\{t\}} (should be [N]\{i\}); typos such as 'coodination' and 'monotonicaly'; and the proof sketch of Theorem 4.1 uses inconsistent notation (e.g., y_{i_t^*} vs y_{i_t^*,t}). There is also no dedicated limitations section despite the strong modeling assumptions (i.i.d. non-strategic outside bids, coordinator with access to private values).

strengths: The paper is the first to study coordination among value-maximizing auto-bidders under RoS constraints, which is a novel and relevant problem in online advertising.

The theoretical results are strong and well-supported: Theorem 3.1 gives a necessary and sufficient condition (Assumption 1) for coordination to improve every bidder's RoS compliance for any overbidding algorithm; Theorem 4.1 shows coordination unconditionally improves total value for mirror-descent auto-bidders; Theorem 4.2 shows asymptotic optimality among all coordination mechanisms under Assumption 1.
The proofs are rigorous, with careful use of potential functions, martingale concentration, and dual envelope arguments. The extension to non-i.i.d. valuations is a useful addition.
Experiments on synthetic and real-world (iPinYou) datasets qualitatively support the theoretical predictions, showing improved utility and value under coordination.
The paper is generally well-written and clear, with a logical structure and helpful proof sketches.
weaknesses: The paper does not discuss the ethical implications of bid coordination, which is closely related to collusion/cartels and can harm outside bidders, reduce platform revenue, and raise antitrust concerns. A broader impact discussion is missing.

The coordination mechanism assumes full information sharing of private values and a central planner, without analyzing incentive compatibility. Bidders may have incentives to misreport values, which limits practical applicability.

Some technical assumptions used in the proofs (e.g., the outside bid distribution D admits a strictly positive density on [0,B]) are not stated in the main theorem statements, creating a gap between the formal results and their presentation.

The real-world data experiment is a synthetic simulation that draws values i.i.d. from the empirical winning-price distribution and scales outside bids, rather than a genuine test of coordination in real auctions. The authors acknowledge this, but it limits the external validity of the empirical support.
There are minor presentation issues: a typo in Eq. (1) (index set should be [N]\{i} rather than [N]\{t}), a broken reference in Theorem 5.2, and some formatting problems in the appendix.
No code or reproducibility package is provided, although the algorithms and experimental settings are described in enough detail to be potentially reproducible.

strengths: Provides a clean formalization of coordinated auto-bidding among value-maximizers under RoS constraints, a setting that is less studied than utility-maximizing bidders, and connects it to the existing collusion/coordination literature.

Theorem 3.1 gives a sharp necessary-and-sufficient condition (Assumption 1) under which the simple highest-value-compete mechanism improves every coalition member's RoS compliance for any weakly-overbidding algorithm, and the matching negative construction (Appendix A.2) is a reasonable (if contrived) necessity argument.

Theorem 4.1 (unconditional value improvement for mirror-descent algorithms) and Theorem 4.2 (asymptotic optimality under Assumption 1) are non-trivial; the virtual-bidder/Lagrangian-envelope argument in Appendix B.1–B.2 is a sensible way to relate the N-bidder dynamics to a single-bidder relaxation.

The extension to independent-but-not-identically-distributed values (Theorems 5.1–5.2) is a useful robustness check, and the honest acknowledgment that individual guarantees do not carry over is appropriate.
weaknesses: Research-ethics / externality concerns are entirely unaddressed. The mechanism is essentially bid-rigging among coalition members, which lowers platform revenue and harms non-coordinating advertisers; the paper neither discusses these externalities nor detection/prevention, legality, or broader impact, and the closing framing ('useful guidance for industrial practice') reads as promoting the practice rather than analyzing it. At minimum an ethics/broader-impact discussion is required.

The 'real-world' experiments are not really real-world. Values are drawn i.i.d. from the pooled empirical winning-price distribution (conflating valuations with prices), and the outside bid is that same distribution rescaled by U[1,2]. This is essentially a synthetic i.i.d. experiment with an empirical distribution and does not substantiate claims about 'realistic market conditions.'

The core conclusions are fairly intuitive: removing intra-coalition competition lowers internal prices (improving RoS) and letting the top-value bidder compete preserves value against outsiders. The theoretical value lies mostly in rigor and the characterization (Assumption 1), not in surprising insight.

Practical assumptions limit reach: the mechanism presumes a central planner that knows all coalition values and can enforce the rule. For the third-party-agent scenario values are private and require elicitation, which the paper relegates to future work, so the motivating scenario is only partially supported.

Empirical evaluation is narrow and confirmatory: every tested distribution conforms to Assumption 1, so the negative/failure regime is never tested, and there is no comparison against alternative baselines (e.g., other coordination mechanisms when Assumption 1 fails) or any platform-side metric such as revenue/efficiency.

Presentation problems: broken equation references (e.g., 'LABEL:eq:coordinated_miR', malformed exponent notation in Theorem 5.2), 'roof sketch' typo, heavy reliance on proof sketches in the main text with the substance buried in a dense appendix, and low-resolution figures that are hard to read.

strengths: Formalizes a novel and timely problem: coordination among value-maximizing auto-bidders under RoS constraints, distinct from prior work on utility maximizers and independent bidding.

Provides sharp theoretical characterization: Assumption 1 is shown to be necessary and sufficient for coordination to improve every coalition bidder's RoS compliance for any weakly overbidding algorithm (Theorem 3.1), with a clear proof via a truthful-bidding benchmark and a matching counterexample when the assumption fails.

Proves unconditional total value improvement for mirror-descent auto-bidders (Theorem 4.1) and asymptotic optimality of the simple highest-value-compete coordination under Assumption 1 (Theorem 4.2), using rigorous mirror-descent dynamics, occupation bounds, and dual-envelope arguments.
Extends the analysis to non-i.i.d. valuations with per-bidder conditions, showing robustness of the coordination benefits at the coalition level (Theorems 5.1 and 5.2).

Experiments on synthetic data and the iPinYou dataset are consistent with the theoretical predictions, with multiple settings and confidence intervals, supporting the practical relevance of the results.
weaknesses: The paper does not discuss the ethical, legal, or market-efficiency implications of bidder coordination. The proposed coalition suppresses competition among its members, which is essentially collusion in auction terms and may harm outside bidders and platform revenue; a broader-impact/ethics discussion is missing.

The real-world experiments do not use actual valuations. Values are sampled from observed winning prices, which are payments rather than private values, and the outside bid is artificially scaled. This limits external validity, and the claim that the results are validated under realistic market conditions is overstated.

The coordination mechanism requires the coalition to know all bidders' private values each round to identify the highest-value bidder. This is a strong informational assumption, especially for a third-party agent coordinating multiple independent advertisers; the paper only acknowledges this limitation in future work.

The theoretical guarantees are asymptotic as T→∞ and assume i.i.d. outside bids. Finite-time performance, strategic or auto-bidding outside bidders, and correlated valuations are not addressed, which restricts practical reach.

Minor technical and presentation issues: Equation (1) uses [N]\{t} instead of [N]\{i}; Lemma B.11 states Δ>0 although Assumption 1 only requires Δ≥0 (fixable but should be corrected); the statement of Theorem 5.2 contains malformed notation; and no code or artifact link is provided for reproducibility.
